raw_response.country: Multi-country (68 countries globally with IMF GFS and UN/WDI data)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines access to drinking water and sanitation services across countries, measured via UN/WDI national, rural, and urban percentages of the population with access to improved sanitation facilities and improved water sources.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this study qualifies ('yes', so plain_criterion2_decision = 'include') because it tests fiscal decentralisation (subnational share of total government revenues and expenditures), political competition (Polity2), bureaucratic quality, democratic accountability, and federal constitutional status. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification, however, it fails ('no'): the exposures are aggregate macro-fiscal decentralisation ratios across all sectors of government (IMF GFS revenue share and expenditure share) and cross-national macro-governance indices (Polity IV, ICRG, federal state dummy), rather than a legal or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical econometric analysis of longitudinal cross-country panel data (68 countries, 1991-2014, ~1,022-1,036 country-year observations) using pooled OLS, Random Effects, and Hausman-Taylor instrumental-variable panel estimators.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports population access outcomes: percentage of total, rural, and urban population with access to improved sanitation facilities and improved drinking water sources.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis (country-year panel across 68 countries from 1991 to 2014), exposures (1-year lagged IMF GFS subnational revenue share and expenditure share, interacted with Polity2 political competition), outcomes (UN/WDI improved water and sanitation access percentages), and observational panel econometric design are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with a Spanish abstract at the end).

evidence_quotes.quote: In the first case, the dependent variable is the percentage of the total population with improved access to sanitation facilities for a country in a particular year. In the second case, the dependent variable is the percentage of the total population with improved access to water sources for a country in a particular year.

Two measures of decentralisation are considered in this study: Revenue share is the subnational governments’ share of revenues as a percentage of total government revenues, and Expenditure share is the subnational governments’ share of expenditures as a percentage of total government expenditures.

The major problem with these measures is the aggregation of data in the GFS. Information at the subnational level is aggregated, making it difficult to account for heterogeneity between tiers and within tiers of government under decentralisation.

Though data on improved access to drinkable water and sanitation is available for almost all the world countries, the sample size for this study is reduced to 68 because some countries did not report any data in GFS.
The data on improved access to sanitation and water is from the UN database reported in World Bank Development Indicators (WDI).

raw_response.exposure: Macro-fiscal decentralisation measured as 1-year lagged subnational government share of total government revenues and expenditures (IMF GFS), interacted with macro-level political competition (Polity2 dummy), plus ICRG bureaucratic quality, democratic accountability, and federal state dummy.
raw_response.outcome: Percentage of national, rural, and urban population with access to improved sanitation facilities and improved drinking water sources (UN/JMP via World Bank WDI).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Unbalanced panel of 68 countries from 1991 to 2014 (1,022 to 1,036 country-year observations; unit of analysis: country-year).
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically estimates the relationship between governance/decentralisation and national/rural/urban water and sanitation access across 68 countries (and would be included under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2), its exposures are economy-wide macro-fiscal decentralisation shares (subnational share of total government revenue and expenditure in IMF GFS) and general cross-national political/institutional indices (Polity2, ICRG bureaucratic quality and democratic accountability, federal constitution dummy). It does not examine a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariffs/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility ownership/regulatory structure).
raw_response.study_design: Observational cross-country longitudinal panel econometric study (pooled OLS, Random Effects, and Hausman-Taylor IV panel estimator, 1991-2014).
